 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. Every tennis season can bring difficult stretches, and Alexandra Eala entered the Ningbo Open looking to regain momentum after a run of disappointing results.
 Comments Eala made earlier in the season reveal a measured approach to competition. She has emphasized improving her level, winning more matches and avoiding rigid ranking targets as she navigates growing expectations on tour.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Why Eala arrived in Ningbo under pressure 
 Alexandra Eala arrived in Ningbo looking to reverse a difficult stretch. She had lost her opening match in Singapore to Tatiana Prozorova after receiving a first-round bye, then fell to Shi Han in the first round in Wuhan. Ningbo offered her a chance to reset.
 Eala entered the tournament ranked No. 20 in the world, having already reached a career-high No. 18 earlier in the season. A strong week in Ningbo could help her regain momentum near the end of a breakthrough year.
 The pressure was not entirely new. Eala has spoken throughout the season about managing expectations and concentrating on the level of tennis she produces rather than setting a rigid ranking target.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Her main goal is winning more matches 
 Eala put it simply: her main focus is to win more matches. She tied that goal to consistently producing a high level and staying healthy throughout a long, demanding season.
 That answer sounds modest, but it carries weight. Wins can build confidence and help a player establish rhythm on court. Consistent results can also lead to ranking gains over time.
 Eala deliberately avoided setting a rigid year-end ranking target. Instead, she described an approach centered on her level of play, match results and health as the season progresses.
 Source: thenews2.com/Depositphotos
 Why rankings are not her priority 
 Earlier this season, Eala said she did not want too much pressure on herself over rankings. She would not name a single position as her goal. She also spoke of balancing tennis with other duties.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Tennis has a lot of numbers to chase. Rankings, seeds, and points can weigh on a young mind. Staying away from those targets lets a player breathe and trust her game when matches get tight.
 Handling a busy life is part of growing up in the spotlight. Fame brings new demands every month. Learning to protect time and energy matters for any young star on the court and off it.
 Eala bounces back with a win over Parry 
 On Monday, Eala beat French player Diane Parry 6-3, 6-1 in the first round. It was her first WTA Tour match win since the US Open in September and ended a 3-match Tour-level losing streak.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Eala controlled the match with consistent tennis and effective returning. She won 55% of Parry's first-serve points and 69% of her second-serve return points while converting 6 of 9 break opportunities.
 For a player who has emphasized winning more matches and producing a consistent level, the victory gave her a positive start to the week in Ningbo.
 Numbers behind her breakout season 
 Eala's progress in 2026 is clear in her results. Before this season, she had recorded 15 career tour-level match wins. Her victory over Diane Parry in Ningbo was already her 34th tour-level win of 2026.
 The season has also produced major milestones. Eala won her first WTA Tour singles title in Washington and climbed as high as No. 18 in the world rankings. Those achievements give her difficult autumn results a much broader context.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Progress rarely follows a straight line, and Ningbo gave Eala an opportunity to regain momentum after her recent losses. Her straight-sets victory over Parry provided exactly that kind of positive result.
 Little-known fact: Eala did not develop a natural throwing motion growing up, which affected her serve toss. She spent months tossing a miniature American football at the Rafa Nadal Academy and back home in Manila, working on her motion.
 Small ranking gains add up fast 
 Eala entered the week at No. 20 in the official WTA rankings. As of Oct. 22, before her second-round match against Diana Shnaider, she had risen to No. 18 in the live rankings.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Live rankings can change throughout a tournament as results and points are updated. Advancing further in Ningbo could strengthen Eala's position heading into the closing weeks of the season.
 Eala has said rankings are not her main focus. Instead, she has emphasized winning more matches and producing a consistent level, with the expectation that ranking progress will follow strong results.
 Source: thenews2.com/Depositphotos
 A close friend may await Eala 
 Eala now faces a round-of-16 match in Ningbo. That is a very big task on its own. A strong showing there could open a path deeper into the draw against some familiar faces.
 Friends often make the toughest opponents on tour. They know each other's habits, strengths and weaknesses very well. That can turn a match into a chess game and a real mental test for both players.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement A meeting would be tough but also very useful for her growth. Beating a rival who knows her game well would show real progress this year. Eala only needs to win the next match first.
 How a young Filipina became a star 
 Eala's rise began well before her current Top 20 status. She started playing tennis at age 4 and later trained at the Rafael Nadal Academy in Mallorca, eventually breaking through on the WTA Tour.
 Her 2025 Miami semifinal made her the first player from the Philippines to reach a WTA 1000 semifinal, and her progress continued in 2026. She won her first WTA Tour title in Washington and reached a career-high ranking of No. 18.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Her approach remains straightforward. Eala has said she wants to win more matches and consistently produce her best level, believing that stronger rankings can follow from those results.
 TL;DR 
 Eala arrived in Ningbo after disappointing exits in Singapore and Wuhan, looking to regain momentum.
 Her stated focus is to win more matches, stay healthy and produce a consistent level.
 She avoids setting rigid ranking targets and has spoken about maintaining balance outside tennis.
 She beat Diane Parry 6-3, 6-1 and stood at No. 18 in the live rankings as of Oct. 22.
 Diana Shnaider is her Round of 16 opponent, while close friend Iva Jovic is a possible quarterfinal opponent.
